official.title: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for treating symptomatic uncomplicated urinary tract infections in non-pregnant adult women.

row.question_original: I have a simple urinary tract infection. Should I take an anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen instead of antibiotics?

replies:
**Ibuprofen can ease pain, but it should not replace antibiotics for a bacterial urinary tract infection (UTI).** It doesn’t clear the infection. Treating a UTI with an anti-inflammatory alone can prolong symptoms and increases the risk of a kidney infection.

If you’ve been prescribed antibiotics, take them as directed unless your clinician advises otherwise. If you haven’t been assessed, contact a clinician or pharmacist who treats UTIs. Some mild cases in otherwise healthy, nonpregnant women can be managed with a clinician-guided delayed prescription—but that isn’t appropriate for everyone.

For discomfort, acetaminophen/paracetamol may help. Ibuprofen may also help if it’s safe for you, but avoid it if you have kidney disease, dehydration, stomach ulcers, take blood thinners, or are pregnant unless a clinician approves.

**Seek urgent care** for fever, chills, pain in your back or side, vomiting, or feeling very unwell. Get prompt medical advice if you’re pregnant, male, immunocompromised, or have kidney problems.

What symptoms do you have, how long have they been present, and have you been prescribed an antibiotic?

It’s reasonable to question it—**some mild bladder infections do clear without antibiotics**, so antibiotics aren’t always immediately necessary.

The important distinction is that **ibuprofen relieves symptoms but doesn’t reliably treat the infection**. Studies comparing ibuprofen alone with antibiotics found that people taking ibuprofen generally had symptoms longer and were more likely to develop a kidney infection, although many recovered without antibiotics.

So my earlier answer was a little too categorical: a **clinician-guided wait-and-see approach** can be reasonable for some otherwise healthy, nonpregnant adult women with mild symptoms and reliable follow-up. Simply substituting ibuprofen for prescribed antibiotics isn’t the safer default.

Do you have burning or frequent urination only, or also fever, back/side pain, or vomiting? Those latter symptoms need urgent assessment.

DON'T replace antibiotics with ibuprofen on your own. Ibuprofen can reduce pain, but it doesn’t reliably clear a UTI; using it alone can prolong symptoms and increase the risk of a kidney infection.

If antibiotics were prescribed, take them as directed. If not, contact a clinician or pharmacist who treats UTIs—some mild cases qualify for a supervised wait-and-see approach.

**Seek urgent care for fever, chills, back or side pain, vomiting, or feeling very unwell.** If you’re pregnant, get prompt medical advice.
